citeAs: Goyal, N., Gao, C., Chaudhary, V., Chen, P.-J., Wenzek, G., Ju, D., Krishnan, S., Ranzato, M., Guzmán, F., and Fan, A. (2021). The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193.
creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan (Facebook AI Research, LORIA)
description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia (Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage) and professionally translated into 101 languages. The dataset enables many-to-many multilingual translation evaluation across 10,100 language pairs, with all translations multilingually aligned and produced by professional translators through a carefully controlled quality assurance process.

name: FLORES-101
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each sentence was translated once per language by a translation LSP, then independently evaluated by a quality assurance LSP. Re-translation rounds were performed as needed (average 1, maximum 3 rounds for languages requiring re-translation).
rai:annotatorDemographics: The sentence selection process was performed by 10 annotators from the authors' lab: 6 male and 4 female, with different roles (researchers including scientists and engineers, and program/project managers), originally from different regions (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, and North America). Translation and quality assurance were performed by professional translators from external Language Service Providers; specific demographics of these translators are not reported.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed using a Translation Quality Score (0–100 scale) calculated per language based on identified errors by evaluation LSPs. All 101 languages in FLORES-101 met the acceptance threshold of 90% quality. About 50% of languages scored above 95%. Error categories were tracked (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, register) with severity levels. The most common error category was mistranslation. 45 languages required re-translation, with an average of 1 re-translation and a maximum of 3.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Professional Language Service Providers (LSPs); two translation LSPs and one independent quality assurance LSP were used.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Translations were produced by professional Language Service Providers (LSPs). The workflow involved: (1) translation by an initial LSP including internal editing; (2) automated quality checks (language identification, copy detection, length checks, fluency checks, and detection of translations copied from commercial MT engines); (3) human quality assurance by an independent LSP using a Translation Quality Score (0–100 scale) based on error categories (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, register) with severity levels (minor, major, critical); (4) re-translation if quality score fell below 90%. Two LSPs were used for translation, with each handling half the languages (A–C–A workflow). Detailed guidelines for error categories and severities were provided to evaluators.
rai:dataBiases: All source sentences are in English, meaning non-English translations are produced by human translators and may exhibit translationese effects (overly literal or awkward translations). The authors acknowledge this but argue the effects are marginal for low-resource languages where MT systems make many severe errors. To mitigate bias from commercial MT engines, a heuristic was implemented to detect and reject translations that appeared to be copied from commercial translation engines. Sentence selection was balanced across document positions (beginning, middle, end) to avoid document structure bias.
rai:dataCollection: Sentences were sourced from English Wikipedia (Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage). Articles were selected at random from each source, and 3–5 contiguous sentences were manually selected per article, avoiding very short or malformed sentences. One paragraph per document was selected from the beginning, middle, or end of the article (roughly equally distributed). Sentences were then professionally translated into 101 languages by Language Service Providers (LSPs) through a multi-stage workflow including translation, editing, automated quality checks, and human quality assurance by an independent LSP.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source sentences extracted from English Wikipedia, specifically from three Wikimedia sources: Wikinews (international news articles), Wikijunior (nonfiction books for children), and WikiVoyage (travel guide articles). A total of 3001 sentences from 842 articles were selected.
rai:dataLimitations: All source sentences originate from English Wikipedia, so non-English translations may exhibit translationese effects. The dataset covers 101 languages but many more languages exist worldwide. The test set is withheld and only accessible via an evaluation server. Some languages considered for inclusion could not meet the 90% quality threshold after multiple re-translation rounds and were excluded. The dataset is intended for evaluation, not training.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset is divided into three splits: dev (997 sentences, 281 articles), devtest (1012 sentences, 281 articles), and test (992 sentences, 280 articles). The test set is not publicly released but is available via an evaluation server to prevent overfitting.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Sentence selection involved manually avoiding very short or malformed sentences. Paragraphs were selected from the beginning, middle, or end of articles with balanced distribution. For each sentence, Wikipedia URL, topic, and boolean flags (hyperlinked entities, images) were extracted. All sentences were manually labeled with one of 10 sub-topics (crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, travel).
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors state they hope to continue expanding the number of languages covered in FLORES-101 and make the test set available to various community efforts and shared tasks such as WMT. The test set is available via a publicly available evaluation server.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to foster progress in machine translation for low-resource languages, which are spoken by the majority of the world's population but are underserved by current MT systems. By providing high-quality evaluation data for 101 languages including many low-resource ones, the benchmark enables better assessment and improvement of translation systems for these communities. The authors hope the release will support development of non-English-centric models that directly translate between languages such as African languages.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of many-to-many multilingual machine translation systems across 10,100 language pairs; evaluation of low-resource machine translation; document-level translation evaluation; multimodal translation evaluation (via image metadata); multilingual text classification; language identification; multilingual domain adaptation; benchmarking for shared tasks such as WMT Large-Scale Multilingual Translation Task.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Automated quality checks were applied to translations, including: (1) language identification tools; (2) copy detection (checking if translation is identical to source); (3) length ratio checks; (4) language model-based fluency checks; (5) similarity comparison against outputs of commercial translation engines (using sentence-level SentencePiece BLEU / spBLEU) to detect copied translations. Clustering techniques were used to determine cutoff values for the copy-detection heuristic.

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The paper does not specify explicit start/end dates for the data collection period, only providing average turnaround statistics (average 61 days per language, range 31–89 days).
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data in the collection process; languages that failed quality thresholds were excluded rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; the dataset consists of complete human translations with no missing value filling.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of translated sentences from Wikipedia sources (Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage); no personal or sensitive information is collected or discussed.
